identification.summary: China-based espionage group that MITRE ATT&CK describes as launching spearphishing campaigns against Japanese and Taiwanese organizations [S2]. In late November and early December 2015, FireEye observed known and suspected China-based APT groups send malicious Word attachments to Japanese and Taiwanese organizations in financial services, high-tech, media and government. The attachments exploited a silently patched Microsoft Office EPS vulnerability plus Windows privilege escalation CVE-2015-1701 and delivered the IRONHALO downloader or the ELMER backdoor [S1][S3]. Press coverage of the FireEye reporting says APT16 sent phishing to Taiwanese news organizations and targeted the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) ahead of Taiwan's January 2016 presidential election [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Publicly reported activity begins about 2015-11-26, when FireEye recorded a spearphishing wave starting around 10:00 AM Japan time [S1]. No earlier activity is established in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: none found. The Microsoft mapping was not checked in this pass, and the actor record has no msName. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as APT16 (G0023) [S2]. Malpedia lists SVCMONDR and G0023 as synonyms [S3]. SecurityWeek, reporting Kaspersky research, describes SVCMONDR as a Kaspersky-named actor that targeted Taiwanese organizations in December 2015, and mentions it separately from APT16 [S5]. Treat the SVCMONDR = APT16 equivalence as a Malpedia mapping, not a Kaspersky statement. Part one of FireEye's 'EPS Awakens' blog, the only primary document opened, does not name APT16. MITRE cites 'EPS Awakens Part 2' for the APT16 attribution [S1][S2].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (suspected). MITRE describes APT16 as China-based [S2]. SCMP reports that FireEye identified APT16 as a China-based, state-backed group [S4]. CFR's Cyber Operations Tracker lists China as the suspected state sponsor [S8].
attribution.confidence: Vendor and tracker assessments only. FireEye/Mandiant made the attribution [S1][S4], and MITRE and CFR repeat it [S2][S8]. No government attribution, indictment or sanction of APT16 was found in the sources gathered. No specific PRC organization (MSS, PLA unit or contractor) is named.
attribution.basis: FireEye's technical analysis of the November-December 2015 EPS exploit campaigns and their payloads [S1]; FireEye statements to press about Taiwan media and DPP targeting [S4]; MITRE ATT&CK group entry [S2].

objectives: Political and economic espionage focused on Japan and Taiwan [S2][S8]. In Taiwan, FireEye analyst Bryce Boland said the attackers were seeking information about the upcoming election and the DPP in particular. FireEye also warned that access to news organizations could expose journalists' informants and protected sources [S4]. Boland's comment is FireEye's assessment of intent.

targeting.notes: FireEye's activity summary covers several China-based groups and gives the sector list for Japan and Taiwan 'respectively', without splitting sectors by group [S1]. CFR and Malpedia apply that combined sector list to APT16 [S3][S8]. The Taiwan media and DPP targeting is tied to APT16 specifically in press reporting of FireEye [S4][S5].

capabilities.summary: Spearphishing with malicious Word documents. In 2015 these exploited a Microsoft Office EPS 'dict copy' use-after-free that had been silently patched on 2015-11-10, so the campaign hit unpatched systems within about two weeks of the fix [S1]. The documents chained a user-mode Office exploit with CVE-2015-1701 for SYSTEM-level privilege escalation [S1]. Payloads were the IRONHALO downloader or the ELMER backdoor (FireEye detection Backdoor.APT.Suroot) [S1]. ELMER is a non-persistent, proxy-aware HTTP backdoor written in Delphi; it can list processes and directories [S9]. APT16 compromised otherwise legitimate websites to stage second-stage payloads [S2]. Social engineering used political lures such as the subject line "DPP's Contact Information Update" [S4]. SecurityWeek reports, citing Kaspersky, that APT16 also used an exploit for the patched EPS flaw CVE-2015-2545 against Taiwanese media and government agencies [S5].

campaigns.name: EPS exploit spearphishing against Japan and Taiwan
campaigns.summary: Known and suspected China-based APT groups sent Word attachments to Japanese and Taiwanese organizations in finance, high-tech, media and government. The attachments chained a silently patched EPS use-after-free with CVE-2015-1701 and dropped IRONHALO or ELMER [S1]. MITRE and Malpedia attribute this activity to APT16, citing FireEye [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Taiwan media and DPP targeting ahead of the 2016 presidential election
campaigns.summary: FireEye reported APT16 phishing Taiwanese news organizations with the lure subject "DPP's Contact Information Update". FireEye assessed the attackers were seeking election- and DPP-related information [S4]. SCMP also reported that DPP staff email accounts were broken into, but this does not show that APT16 did it [S4].

campaigns.name: SVCMONDR activity against Taiwan (Kaspersky naming)
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky, as reported by SecurityWeek, observed actors exploiting CVE-2015-2545, including APT16 against Taiwanese media and government agencies, and a threat actor it named SVCMONDR against Taiwanese organizations in December 2015 [S5][S6]. Malpedia treats SVCMONDR as an APT16 alias [S3].

diamond.adversary: APT16, a China-based group that FireEye describes as state-backed. No named organization or individuals [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Office EPS exploit chained with CVE-2015-1701 for privilege escalation; IRONHALO downloader; ELMER Delphi HTTP backdoor [S1][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites used as staging servers for second-stage payloads [S2]; HTTP command and control for ELMER [S9]. Specific domains and IPs were not captured in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Japanese and Taiwanese organizations in media, government, finance and high-tech; Taiwan news outlets and the DPP [S1][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on Taiwan's opposition party and the media around the January 2016 presidential election, a period of high PRC interest in Taiwan's political direction [S4].
diamond.technology: Microsoft Office's EPS filter and Windows privilege escalation on hosts that had not applied the November 2015 updates [S1].

gaps: Could not open FireEye 'The EPS Awakens - Part 2', the document that names APT16 and gives operational detail. Its URL was not found, and the guessed Google Cloud paths returned 404. Part one, which was opened, does not name APT16 [S1].
MITRE ATT&CK, Malpedia, CFR, SecurityWeek, SCMP, Securelist and CNN pages could not be fetched (DNS or proxy blocks). Their content here comes from search-result summaries.

The SVCMONDR alias conflicts between sources: Malpedia lists it as an APT16 synonym [S3], while SecurityWeek's coverage of Kaspersky names SVCMONDR alongside APT16 as an apparently separate actor [S5].
The claim that APT16 sent phishing from a compromised Taiwanese government email account could not be verified in the sources gathered and is excluded.
Third-party blogs claim activity since 2012, an 'OpTaiwan' alias and a June 2015 DOORJAMB lure. None of these is corroborated by primary sources, so all are excluded.
In June 2016, CNN reported a compromise of the DPP website. The coverage says FireEye did not link it to APT16 [S7].
No public reporting on APT16 after 2016 was found. It is unknown whether the group was retired, renamed or merged into another cluster.
No Microsoft (Typhoon) name or government attribution was found.
No IOCs (domains, hashes) were captured. IRONHALO's functionality beyond 'downloader' is undocumented in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Taiwan and Japan political, media and government networks around elections and policy events. Where US forces work with Japanese and Taiwanese partners, those networks are relevant terrain [S1][S4]. STEP 2 (effects): Weaponizing an Office flaw about two weeks after a silent patch shows that patch lag on partner and media networks creates exploitable windows [S1]. STEP 3 (threat model): The sequence is a political-themed spearphish, then a Word EPS exploit, then CVE-2015-1701 privilege escalation, then IRONHALO or ELMER, with second stages staged on compromised legitimate sites [S1][S2][S4]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is espionage against Taiwanese and Japanese political, media and government targets timed to elections or crises. MDCOA is use of media access to identify sources and shape or pre-empt reporting during a Taiwan Strait crisis [S4]. Candidate indicators: Word attachments with embedded EPS content; Office processes spawning executables followed by privilege escalation; HTTP beacons from Delphi binaries through proxies; downloads of second-stage payloads from otherwise reputable websites [S1][S2][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: The group has no public reporting after 2016, so treat APT16 as a historical TTP baseline for PRC election-period targeting of Taiwan and Japan, not as a current tracked threat [S1][S4]. (2) Authorities: Victims were partner-nation media, political parties and government entities. Any response runs through partner and interagency channels, not DoD network authorities [S4]. (3) Mission assurance: Confirm Office and Windows patch currency on systems shared with partners, since this actor used a vulnerability silently patched two weeks earlier [S1]. (4) Coordination: Reconcile vendor naming (APT16, SVCMONDR, G0023) before sharing indicators with partners to avoid double-counting [S3][S5].
